summary: On win32, test 5 asserts powershellCalls is empty, but spawnTerminalAgent calls readAgentStartTime on the mocked child pid 2147483647. The in-process reader returns undefined for that nonexistent pid, so the code falls back to windowsProcessQuery and calls PowerShell, and the assertion fails on the Windows free-tests CI.
evidence: Fake Bun.spawn returns { pid: 2147483647 }; terminal-agent-control.ts:73 `return win32CreationTimeSource.read(pid) ?? windowsProcessQuery(pid).startTime;`. A scratch repro (platform faked as win32, reader returning a value only for process.pid, spawnTerminalAgent called the same way) printed: powershell calls: [ "-NoProfile -NonInteractive -Command (Get-CimInstance Win32_Process -Filter 'ProcessId = 2147483647' ...)" ] and the test failed (0 pass, 1 fail).

summary: win32CreationTimeSource.read returns a creation time for a process that has exited but still has open handles, because the GetProcessTimes exit time (times[1]) is ignored. The terminal-agent owner watchdog checks only readAgentStartTime equality, with no aliveness check, so a crashed owner whose process object is still referenced looks alive and the agent never cleans up. The old CIM/PowerShell path returned '' for exited processes.
evidence: Line 55: `if (!win32Kernel.GetProcessTimes(handle, ptr(times, 0), ptr(times, 8), ...) || times[0] === 0n) return;` never checks times[1]. terminal-agent.ts:1187: `if (!BROWSE_OWNER_START_TIME || readAgentStartTime(BROWSE_OWNER_PID) !== BROWSE_OWNER_START_TIME || ...) void cleanup();` has no isProcessAlive guard, unlike agentStatus (line 366), which calls isAgentRecordLive first. Fix: return undefined when times[1] !== 0n, or require GetExitCodeProcess == STILL_ACTIVE (259). Not confirmed on Windows; this environment is Linux.
